overview.title: Learning as feedback-driven adjustment; representations and the coordinate-change example
overview.section: 1.4 Learning rules and representations from data
overview.main_topic: The definition of learning as adjustment from a feedback signal, the notion of a representation (RGB vs. HSV), and the black/white points example in which a coordinate change produces a representation that makes classification easy (figures 1.3 and 1.4)
overview.central_idea: Learning is the adjustment of an algorithm using the measured distance between its outputs and the expected outputs as a feedback signal. The central problem of machine learning and deep learning is to transform data meaningfully — to learn useful *representations* of the input that bring us closer to the expected output. A representation is a different way of encoding the same data, and a task hard in one representation can be easy in another; a rotation of the axes in figure 1.4 turns a tangled two-colour point cloud into one separable by a single rule.
overview.importance: This page introduces the idea that organizes the whole book: a model is a learned transformation to a better representation. Everything later — layers, embeddings, convolutional feature maps, latent spaces — is a representation in this sense. The coordinate-change example is the simplest possible instance and is reused on p.30 to define learning as a search over transformations.
learning_objectives: Define learning as the adjustment step driven by a feedback signal
State the central problem of machine learning and deep learning in terms of representations
Define a representation and give the RGB/HSV example of two representations of the same data, with a task that is easy in each
Map the black/white points problem onto the three ingredients from p.28 (inputs, expected outputs, measure of success)
Explain how the coordinate change in figure 1.4 produces a representation that cleanly separates the two classes
prerequisites: The three ingredients of machine learning: input data, expected outputs, a measure of success (p.28)
Figure 1.2: machine learning finds rules from data and answers (p.28)

summary:
The page finishes the third ingredient from p.28: the measurement of how far the algorithm's output is from the expected output is used as a **feedback signal** to adjust how the algorithm works, and *this adjustment step is what we call learning*.

A machine learning model transforms its input data into meaningful outputs, a process learned from exposure to known examples of inputs and outputs. So the **central problem** of machine learning and deep learning is to *meaningfully transform data* — to learn useful **representations** of the input that get us closer to the expected output.

A representation is a different way to look at, represent or encode data. Example: a colour image can be encoded as **RGB** (red-green-blue) or **HSV** (hue-saturation-value) — two representations of the same data. Some tasks are hard in one and easy in the other: "select all red pixels" is simpler in RGB; "make the image less saturated" is simpler in HSV. Machine learning models are all about finding representations that make the data more amenable to the task.

The concrete example (**figure 1.3**): points in an $(x, y)$ plane, some white and some black, and the goal of an algorithm that takes a point's coordinates and outputs whether it is likely black or white. In the language of p.28:

- the **inputs** are the coordinates of the points;
- the **expected outputs** are the colours of the points;
- a **measure of success** could be the percentage of points correctly classified.

What is needed is a new representation that cleanly separates white from black points. One transformation among many is a **coordinate change**, shown in **figure 1.4** in three panels: (1) raw data, where the two colours form two tilted bands that no axis-aligned rule separates; (2) a new pair of rotated axes drawn over the data; (3) the better representation, where in the new coordinates the black points lie on one side of the vertical axis and the white points on the other. The next page (p.30) states the resulting rule — black points have $x > 0$ — and asks whether such a transformation could be found automatically rather than by hand.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Completing the third bullet from p.28: the measurement of the distance between current and expected output is used as a feedback signal to adjust how the algorithm works, and this adjustment step is what the book calls learning.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Learning is given an operational definition: not 'understanding' but *adjustment in response to a measured error*. Three parts: a measurement (how wrong), a feedback path (the measurement reaches the algorithm), and an adjustment (the algorithm changes). Section 1.6 (p.32–33) will name the parts — loss score, optimizer, weights.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This definition is what makes learning implementable as a loop that a computer can run, and it is the definition used everywhere in the book.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Learning loop: compute output → measure distance to expected output → adjust the algorithm to reduce the distance → repeat.

terminology.meaning: The measured discrepancy between the algorithm's output and the expected output, fed back to drive adjustment.
The adjustment step that changes how the algorithm works in response to the feedback signal.

connections: p.28: the three ingredients, of which the measure is the third.
p.32–33: section 1.6 shows the loop with weights, loss score and optimizer.

paragraphs.excerpt: A machine learning model transforms its input data into meaningful outputs, a
paragraphs.what_it_says: A model transforms inputs into meaningful outputs, a transformation learned from known input/output examples. Therefore the central problem of machine learning and deep learning is to meaningfully transform data — to learn useful representations of the input that get closer to the expected output.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This reframes 'finding rules' (p.28) as 'finding transformations'. The output of a model is itself just another representation of the input — one in which the answer is easy to read off. So learning rules and learning representations are the same activity viewed from two sides.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is the thesis statement of the section and arguably of the book: deep learning will be defined (p.31) as learning *successive* representations, and Chapter 2 (p.43) describes layers as filters that extract more useful representations.
paragraphs.technical_idea: A model is a function $f$ with $f(\text{input}) \to \text{representation}$ such that the expected output becomes a simple function of the representation.

terminology.meaning: A way of encoding data; a model's job is to produce representations that make the task easy.

connections: p.31: deep learning defined as learning successive layers of increasingly meaningful representations.
p.43: layers described as filters that extract representations that are more meaningful for the problem.

paragraphs.excerpt: Before we go any further, what's a representation? At its core, it's a
paragraphs.what_it_says: A representation is a different way to look at, represent or encode data. A colour image can be encoded as RGB or as HSV: two representations of the same data. Tasks that are hard in one can be easy in the other — 'select all red pixels' is simpler in RGB, 'make the image less saturated' is simpler in HSV. Machine learning models are all about finding representations that make the data more amenable to the task.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The RGB/HSV example shows that a representation adds no information — both encode the same image — but changes *what is easy to compute*. In RGB, 'red' is roughly 'large R, small G and B', a threshold on raw channels; in HSV, saturation is a single coordinate, so reducing it is one multiplication. The right representation turns a hard rule into a trivial one.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It gives the reader a precise, non-mystical meaning for 'representation' before the term is used for the internal states of neural networks.
paragraphs.technical_idea: RGB and HSV are related by an invertible transformation; the information is identical, the geometry is different. A 'useful' representation is one in which the quantity you care about is a simple function (ideally one coordinate or one threshold).

terminology.meaning: Encoding of a pixel's colour as red, green and blue intensities.
Encoding of a pixel's colour as hue, saturation and value (brightness).

connections: p.260: in a convnet the channels axis starts as RGB and later channels stand for learned filters — representations learned rather than chosen.

paragraphs.excerpt: Let's make this concrete. Consider an x-axis, a y-axis, and some points
paragraphs.what_it_says: Figure 1.3 shows points with $(x, y)$ coordinates, some white and some black. The goal is an algorithm that takes a point's coordinates and outputs whether it is likely black or white. In the terms of p.28: the inputs are the coordinates, the expected outputs are the colours, and a measure of success could be the percentage of points correctly classified (bullets e04, e05, e07).
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is the smallest possible supervised classification problem: 2-D inputs, binary labels, accuracy as the metric. In figure 1.3 the white points lie in a band running from lower-left to upper-right and the black points in a parallel band to their upper-right, so no rule of the form 'x > c' or 'y > c' on the original axes separates them.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: A toy problem makes the abstract claim about representations visible: you can *see* why the raw coordinates are a poor representation and what a better one looks like.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Inputs $(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$; targets $\in \{\text{black}, \text{white}\}$; measure = fraction of points whose predicted colour matches the true colour.

terminology.meaning: Predicting a category (here black or white) for each input.

connections: p.30: the problem is solved with the rule 'black points are such that x > 0' in the new coordinates.

paragraphs.excerpt: What we need here is a new representation of our data that cleanly
paragraphs.what_it_says: What is needed is a new representation that cleanly separates white from black points. One transformation among many possibilities is a coordinate change, illustrated in figure 1.4.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Figure 1.4 has three panels: raw data; the same data with a new pair of rotated axes drawn through the gap between the two bands; and the data re-plotted in those new axes, where the black points sit to the right of the new vertical axis and the white points to the left. The transformation moved no information — it only re-expressed each point in coordinates aligned with the structure of the problem. 'Among many other possibilities' foreshadows p.30, where learning is described as a search over a space of such transformations.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the first concrete picture of what a model does: change coordinates so that a simple rule works. Dense layers do exactly this in higher dimensions (p.133: a layer projects input onto a representation space).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: a rotation of the axes by angle $\theta$ maps $(x, y)$ to $(x', y') = (x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta,\; -x\sin\theta + y\cos\theta)$; choosing $\theta$ so that the boundary between the bands becomes the line $x' = 0$ yields the rule on p.30.

terminology.meaning: Re-expressing each point's position relative to new axes; a transformation that preserves the data but changes its representation.

connections: p.30: in the new coordinates the rule 'black points are such that x > 0' solves the problem; the authors then ask whether the change could be found automatically.
p.133: a Dense layer's dot product with W projects input onto a new representation space — a learned coordinate change.

concepts.name: Learning (as feedback-driven adjustment)
concepts.definition: The adjustment step in which a measurement of the distance between the algorithm's current output and the expected output is used as a feedback signal to change the way the algorithm works.
concepts.intuition: Measure how wrong you are, nudge yourself to be less wrong, repeat.
concepts.technical: Requires a measurable discrepancy and a mechanism for adjustment; in neural networks the discrepancy is the loss and the adjustment updates the weights (p.32–33).
concepts.significance: This operational definition is what lets learning run as an automatic loop rather than a human activity.
concepts.example: In the points problem, adjusting the coordinate change until the percentage of correctly classified points stops improving.
concepts.misconception: That learning means memorizing the examples; it means changing a transformation so that outputs move toward expected outputs.

concepts.name: Representation
concepts.definition: A different way to look at, represent or encode data; machine learning models are about finding representations of their input that make the data more amenable to the task at hand.
concepts.intuition: Same information, different coordinates — and in the right coordinates the answer is obvious.
concepts.technical: Representations are related by transformations (RGB↔HSV, a rotation of axes). A useful representation is one in which the expected output is a simple function of the coordinates.
concepts.significance: The central problem of machine learning and deep learning is to learn useful representations; deep learning is defined on p.31 as learning them in successive layers.
concepts.example: RGB vs. HSV: selecting red pixels is simpler in RGB, desaturating is simpler in HSV. The rotated coordinates of figure 1.4 make black/white separable by one threshold.
concepts.misconception: That a better representation contains more information. RGB and HSV, or the two coordinate systems in figure 1.4, contain exactly the same information; what differs is which operations are easy.

concepts.name: Coordinate change as a transformation
concepts.definition: Re-expressing data points relative to a new set of axes; in figure 1.4 this transformation turns an inseparable-looking point cloud into one where black and white points lie on opposite sides of an axis.
concepts.intuition: Tilt your head until the dividing line looks vertical.
concepts.technical: A linear transformation of the inputs (here a rotation). Dense layers in later chapters perform learned linear transformations followed by nonlinearities, generalizing this idea to many dimensions (p.133).
concepts.significance: It is the simplest example of a data transformation that produces a better representation, and the model problem for defining learning as a search over transformations (p.30).
concepts.misconception: That the coordinate change moves the points apart; it only changes how their positions are described.

concepts.name: Feedback signal
concepts.definition: The measurement of the distance between the algorithm's current output and its expected output, used to adjust the algorithm.
concepts.intuition: The score that tells the learner which way to change.
concepts.technical: In the points example the percentage of correctly classified points; in neural networks the loss score computed by the loss function (p.33).
concepts.significance: It closes the loop between data+answers and the rules being learned (figure 1.2).
concepts.example: Percentage of points correctly classified as black or white.
concepts.misconception: That accuracy is always the signal used for adjustment; the book later explains why smooth losses, not accuracy, drive gradient-based adjustment (Chapter 2–3).

deeper.title: The coordinate change written out (not in the book)
deeper.body:
The book draws the coordinate change but gives no formula. Beyond the book, a rotation of the axes by an angle $\theta$ sends a point $(x, y)$ to

$$x' = x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta, \qquad y' = -x\sin\theta + y\cos\theta.$$

In figure 1.4 the two bands run from lower-left to upper-right and the gap between them is a diagonal line; the authors draw the new $x'$ axis perpendicular to that gap, so $x'$ measures each point's offset from the gap. Black points (the upper-right band) get $x' > 0$ and white points (the lower-left band) get $x' < 0$. Numerically, suppose the gap runs along $y = x$ and take $\theta = -45^\circ$ ($\cos\theta \approx 0.707$, $\sin\theta \approx -0.707$), so $x' = 0.707\,(x - y)$. A black point at $(2, 1)$ gives $x' = 0.707 \times 1 = 0.71 > 0$; a white point at $(1, 2)$ gives $x' = 0.707 \times (-1) = -0.71 < 0$. One threshold on $x'$ — the rule 'black if $x' > 0$' stated on p.30 — classifies both correctly.

The lesson is not the trigonometry: it is that the whole 'intelligence' of the classifier sits in choosing $\theta$. Learning (p.30) is the automatic search for that choice using the percentage-correct feedback signal.

deeper.title: RGB vs. HSV as a worked example of 'easy in one, hard in the other'
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, make the page's colour example concrete. A pure red pixel is $(R, G, B) = (255, 0, 0)$ and, in HSV, $(H, S, V) = (0^\circ, 1, 1)$.

- **Select all red pixels**: in RGB, test something like $R > 200$ and $G, B < 80$ — a direct threshold on stored numbers. In HSV you would have to test that $H$ is near $0^\circ$ *and* that $S$ and $V$ are high, because low saturation makes any hue look grey; the rule is clumsier.
- **Make the image less saturated**: in HSV, replace $S$ by $0.5\,S$ for every pixel — one coordinate changes. In RGB you must move each pixel toward its own grey level, which requires computing that grey level first and adjusting all three channels.

Neither format knows more about the image. Each simply exposes a different quantity as a single coordinate. This is exactly what a learned representation does for a task: it exposes the quantity the task depends on.

deeper.title: Why the three ingredients reappear in the points example
deeper.body:
The page deliberately restates the p.28 checklist for the toy problem:

1. **Inputs** — the $(x, y)$ coordinates of each point.
2. **Expected outputs** — each point's colour, black or white.
3. **Measure of success** — the percentage of points correctly classified.

Only after all three are fixed does the question 'which transformation?' make sense, because the measure is what judges a transformation. Try it: without item 3, how would you decide that the rotated axes in figure 1.4 are better than the original ones? With it, the answer is immediate — in the new representation a single threshold classifies (nearly) 100% of points correctly, whereas no axis-aligned threshold does so in the raw representation.

misconceptions.claim: A better representation of the data adds information about it.
misconceptions.correction: RGB and HSV encode exactly the same image, and the rotated coordinates in figure 1.4 describe exactly the same points. A better representation changes what is easy to compute, not what is known.

misconceptions.claim: Learning means the model memorizes which answer goes with which input.
misconceptions.correction: The page defines learning as an adjustment step driven by a feedback signal: the model's transformation is changed so that its outputs move closer to the expected outputs.

misconceptions.claim: The coordinate change in figure 1.4 physically separates the black and white points.
misconceptions.correction: The points do not move relative to each other; only the axes change. In the new axes the existing separation happens to align with a single coordinate, so a one-threshold rule works.

earlier.note: The three ingredients of machine learning, the third of which (a measure of success) is completed at the top of this page.

later.note: The new representation yields the rule 'black points are such that x > 0'; the authors ask whether such transformations could be found automatically, leading to learning as a search in a hypothesis space.
Deep learning defined as learning successive layers of increasingly meaningful representations.
Figure 1.6: deep representations learned by a digit classifier — the multistage version of this page's single coordinate change.
Layers as data filters that extract more useful representations.
A Dense layer's dot product with W projects input onto a representation space — a learned, higher-dimensional coordinate change.
Feature engineering: choosing a representation by hand, as the authors do here with the coordinate change.
Convnet feature maps: channels that start as RGB become learned filters.

takeaways: Learning is the adjustment step in which the measured distance between output and expected output is used as a feedback signal to change how the algorithm works.
The central problem of machine learning and deep learning is to meaningfully transform data — to learn useful representations that bring the input closer to the expected output.
A representation is a different way to encode the same data (RGB vs. HSV); a task hard in one representation can be easy in another.

In the black/white points problem, a coordinate change (figure 1.4) is a transformation that produces a representation in which the two classes are cleanly separated — one of many possible transformations.

questions.question: How does the page define learning?
questions.answer: As the adjustment step: the measurement of the distance between the algorithm's output and the expected output is used as a feedback signal to adjust the way the algorithm works, and that adjustment is what we call learning.
questions.explanation: The first sentences of the page complete the third ingredient from p.28 with this operational definition, which section 1.6 later implements with a loss score and an optimizer.

questions.question: Which task does the page say is simpler in the HSV representation than in RGB?
options: Select all red pixels in the image
questions.explanation: The page says 'Select all red pixels in the image' is simpler in RGB, whereas 'Make the image less saturated' is simpler in HSV because saturation is one of HSV's coordinates. Counting pixels and grayscale conversion are not discussed on the page.

questions.question: According to the page, what is the central problem of machine learning and deep learning, and how does the RGB/HSV example illustrate it?
questions.answer: To meaningfully transform data — to learn useful representations of the input that get closer to the expected output. RGB and HSV are two representations of the same image; some tasks are easy in one and hard in the other, showing that choosing the right representation is what makes a task tractable.
questions.explanation: The page states the central problem explicitly and then defines representation with the RGB/HSV example precisely to show that the representation, not the information content, determines how easy a task is.

questions.question: In the black/white points example, which of the following is the 'measure of whether our algorithm is doing a good job' the page proposes?
options: The percentage of points that are correctly classified
The distance between the black and white points
The number of coordinate changes tried
The sum of the x and y coordinates
questions.answer: The percentage of points that are correctly classified
questions.explanation: The third bullet says the measure 'could be, for instance, the percentage of points that are being correctly classified'. The other options are not proposed on the page; the distance between points is a property of the data, not of the algorithm's performance.

questions.question: Explain what the coordinate change in figure 1.4 does and does not do to the data.
questions.answer: It re-expresses each point in a new, rotated coordinate system so that the boundary between black and white points aligns with an axis, making the classes separable by a simple rule (p.30: black points have x > 0). It does not move the points relative to each other or add any information; it only changes the representation.
questions.explanation: The page calls the coordinate change 'a new representation of our data that cleanly separates the white points from the black points' and panel 3 of figure 1.4 shows the same points with the vertical axis now dividing the classes. Since a representation is just a different encoding, information is unchanged.

questions.question: Map the black/white points problem onto the three ingredients of machine learning from p.28.
questions.answer: Inputs: the (x, y) coordinates of the points. Expected outputs: the colours of the points. Measure of success: for instance, the percentage of points correctly classified.
questions.explanation: The three bullets on the page restate the p.28 checklist for this specific problem.

questions.question: Look at panel 1 of figure 1.4. Can you convince yourself that no rule of the form 'x > c' or 'y > c' on the original axes separates the black and white points, and then see why the rotated axes fix this?
questions.answer: In the raw data both colours span overlapping ranges of x and of y, because the bands run diagonally; any horizontal or vertical cut mixes the classes. Rotating the axes so one axis runs along the gap between the bands makes the perpendicular coordinate separate them with a single threshold.
questions.explanation: Self-assessment: the exercise rehearses the page's claim that a task hard in one representation becomes easy in another. The widget on this page lets you apply the rotation yourself.
